subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

questions.q: Fixed charged objects produce an electric potential V at point P. A small particle with charge +q is placed at P and then replaced by a particle with charge −2q. Which statement about the electric potential at P is correct?
options: V reverses sign and doubles, since it is the particle's energy at P
V is unchanged, since the fixed charges set it, not the particle
V reverses sign and halves, because V = U_E/q and q is now −2q
V changes sign but keeps its size, since the particle is negative
optionWhy: A student who takes the potential to be the potential energy of the particle placed at P picks this. That describes U_E = qV, which does double and reverse sign; V is the energy per unit charge and does not depend on the particle.

The potential at P is the potential energy per unit charge, set by the fixed source charges and the position of P. Replacing +q by −2q changes U_E = qV (it doubles in size and changes sign), but V itself is unchanged.
A student who reads V = U_E/q as saying V is inversely proportional to the particle's charge picks this. When q becomes −2q, U_E becomes −2 times as large, so the ratio V stays the same.
A student who thinks the sign of the potential is set by the charge placed at P picks this. The sign of V comes from the fixed source charges; the particle's sign affects only the sign of U_E.
questions.explain: The potential at P is the potential energy per unit charge, set by the fixed source charges and the position of P. Replacing +q by −2q changes U_E = qV (it doubles in size and changes sign), but V itself is unchanged.

questions.q: For two points A and B in an electric field, V_B − V_A = −50 V. Which statement is correct?
options: A charged object moved from A to B changes U_E by −50 J, whatever its charge
A −1.0 C charge moved from A to B lowers U_E by 50 J, as B is at lower potential
U_E falls by 50 J per coulomb on the straight path, and by more on a longer, curved path
If a +1.0 C charge were moved from A to B, by any path, U_E would change by −50 J
optionWhy: A student who thinks the change in potential energy is set by the points alone picks this. −50 V is −50 J per coulomb: ΔU_E = qΔV depends on the charge moved.
A student who thinks every charge loses potential energy moving toward lower potential picks this. For a negative charge ΔU_E = (−1.0 C)(−50 V) = +50 J: U_E increases.
A student who thinks the potential difference depends on the path picks this, expecting a longer path to change U_E more. ΔV between two points, and so ΔU_E per coulomb, is the same for every path.
The potential difference is the change in U_E per unit charge: ΔU_E = qΔV = (+1.0 C)(−50 V) = −50 J, for any path from A to B.
questions.explain: The potential difference is the change in U_E per unit charge: ΔU_E = qΔV = (+1.0 C)(−50 V) = −50 J, for any path from A to B.
questions.working: ΔV = ΔU_E/q, so ΔU_E = qΔV. For q = +1.0 C: ΔU_E = (1.0 C)(−50 V) = −50 J, the same for every path. For q = −1.0 C: ΔU_E = +50 J (U_E increases).

questions.q: A battery maintains a potential difference between its terminals. Which statement correctly describes how it does this?
options: Chemical reactions create new positive and negative charge at the two terminals
It releases stored charge, and it goes dead once the stored charge runs out
Chemical reactions move positive and negative charges apart, to opposite terminals
It pushes out a fixed current, and that current sets the potential difference
optionWhy: A student who thinks a battery makes charge picks this. Charge is conserved: the reactions move existing charges apart, and the battery's net charge stays zero.
A student who pictures a battery as a tank of charge picks this. A battery runs down when its chemical reactants are used up; it does not run out of charge.

Chemical processes inside the battery separate positive and negative charges, making one terminal positive and the other negative. That separation of charge produces the potential difference between the terminals.
A student who thinks a battery supplies a fixed current picks this. An ideal battery maintains a potential difference; the current depends on what is connected to it.
questions.explain: Chemical processes inside the battery separate positive and negative charges, making one terminal positive and the other negative. That separation of charge produces the potential difference between the terminals.

questions.q: The emf ε of a battery is sometimes called its electromotive force. Which of the following correctly describes the emf?
options: A force, in newtons, that the battery exerts on each charge carrier to push it along the wires of the circuit
A current, in amperes, that the battery delivers unchanged to any circuit that is connected to it
An amount of charge, in coulombs, that the battery stores and then releases into the connected circuit
A potential difference, in volts, that the battery maintains and that drives charge around a circuit
optionWhy: A student who takes the word 'force' literally picks this. The emf is measured in volts (joules per coulomb): it is a potential difference, not a force.
A student who thinks a battery is a source of a fixed current picks this. A battery maintains a potential difference; the current it delivers depends on the circuit connected to it.

A student who thinks a battery stores the charge that flows picks this. The charge carriers are already in the wires and other elements; the battery moves them, and its emf is a potential difference, in volts, not an amount of charge.

Despite its name, emf is a potential difference: the energy per unit charge, in volts, that the battery supplies by maintaining a potential difference between its terminals. The charge carriers already in the wires move around the circuit in response to it.
questions.explain: Despite its name, emf is a potential difference: the energy per unit charge, in volts, that the battery supplies by maintaining a potential difference between its terminals. The charge carriers already in the wires move around the circuit in response to it.

questions.q: Wire X is not connected to anything. Wire Y, made of the same metal and at the same temperature, carries a steady current. How does the motion of the free electrons in X compare with that in Y?
options: Their average speeds are about equal, but only in Y is their average velocity not zero.
They are at rest in X, while in Y they all move along the wire at the small drift speed.
Their average speeds are about equal, and in Y those high speeds are directed along the wire.
No electrons in wire X are free to move; in wire Y, electrons supplied by a battery drift.
optionWhy: In both wires the free electrons move in random directions at high speeds, of order 10⁶ m/s, so their average speeds are about the same. In X the random velocities average to zero; in Y the current adds a small drift velocity, of order 10⁻⁴ m/s, along the wire. The current changes the average velocity, not noticeably the average speed.

A student who thinks free electrons are at rest when there is no current picks this. Zero current means zero net motion of charge, not zero speed: the electrons in X move rapidly in random directions, as do those in Y.

A student who thinks the electrons' high speeds are directed along the wire when there is a current picks this. Even in Y the motion is almost entirely random; only a tiny drift velocity, of order 10⁻⁴ m/s, is along the wire.
A student who thinks a wire has no mobile charge until a battery supplies it picks this. Free electrons are present in any metal, connected or not; a battery only makes them drift.
questions.explain: In both wires the free electrons move in random directions at high speeds, of order 10⁶ m/s, so their average speeds are about the same. In X the random velocities average to zero; in Y the current adds a small drift velocity, of order 10⁻⁴ m/s, along the wire. The current changes the average velocity, not noticeably the average speed.

questions.q: A long copper wire connected across a battery carries a steady current. A student recalls that the electric field inside a conductor is zero. Which statement about the electric field inside this wire is correct?
options: It is zero, as inside every conductor; the charge carriers keep on drifting because nothing acts to stop them.
It is zero in the interior; there is a field just at the surface, which is where the current flows.
It is not zero: charge is moving, so the wire is not in electrostatic equilibrium, and a field drives it.
It is not zero near the battery alone, where it pushes carriers that then push the rest along the wire.
optionWhy: A student who applies the electrostatic result to a conductor carrying a current picks this. The steady current requires a field E = ρJ throughout the wire; without it the current would not continue.

A student who carries over the idea that charge on a conductor resides on its surface picks this. In a uniform wire the current is spread over the whole cross section, and so is the field that drives it.

The field inside a conductor is zero only in electrostatic equilibrium, when no charge moves. Here the battery maintains a potential difference along the wire, and the field E = ρJ acts on the carriers everywhere in the wire, keeping them drifting.
A student who pictures the battery pushing charges only at its terminals picks this. There is a field all along the wire: E = ρJ, and J is the same in every part of a uniform wire.
questions.explain: The field inside a conductor is zero only in electrostatic equilibrium, when no charge moves. Here the battery maintains a potential difference along the wire, and the field E = ρJ acts on the carriers everywhere in the wire, keeping them drifting.

questions.q: Which of the following describes a short circuit?
options: A conducting path along which charge flows while its two ends remain at the same potential
A break in a circuit, such as a cut in a wire, across which charge is not able to flow at all
A conducting path whose two ends are at the same potential, so that no charge flows along it
A wire added across one element, which changes that element and nothing else in the circuit
optionWhy: In a short circuit charge flows through a path, such as an ideal wire, with no change in potential from one end to the other. Connected across an element, it holds the element's terminals at the same potential.

A student who takes 'short circuit' in its everyday sense of a fault that stops a device working picks this. A short circuit is the opposite of a break: it is a path through which charge flows easily, with no change in potential.

A student who thinks that charge can flow only where there is a potential difference picks this. An ideal wire carries charge with no potential difference between its ends; that is what makes it a short circuit.

A student who thinks a change in one part of a circuit affects only that part picks this. A wire across one element changes potentials elsewhere: for example, when one of two bulbs in series is shorted, the other has the battery's whole potential difference across it.
questions.explain: In a short circuit charge flows through a path, such as an ideal wire, with no change in potential from one end to the other. Connected across an element, it holds the element's terminals at the same potential.

questions.q: Which information about a circuit does a circuit schematic diagram represent?
options: Which terminals are joined by wires, since connections set its behavior
How long each wire is, since longer wires carry less current to the elements
The order in which current reaches elements, since earlier ones get more of it
The paths that electrons follow, since its arrows show where they move
optionWhy: The connections, not the drawing, determine the circuit's currents and potential differences. A schematic represents how the elements are connected: which terminals are joined by wires. The shapes, positions and lengths of the drawn wires carry no information, and any current arrows show conventional current.
A student who thinks drawn wire lengths matter picks this. Wires in a schematic are ideal; a schematic shows connections, not lengths.

A student who thinks elements that the current reaches earlier receive more of it picks this. Elements in series carry the same current whatever their order; a schematic shows connections, not an order.

A student who reads arrows on schematics as the direction of electron motion picks this. Unless otherwise specified, schematics are drawn using conventional current, the direction positive charge would move, opposite to the electrons' motion in metal wires.
questions.explain: The connections, not the drawing, determine the circuit's currents and potential differences. A schematic represents how the elements are connected: which terminals are joined by wires. The shapes, positions and lengths of the drawn wires carry no information, and any current arrows show conventional current.

questions.q: In a circuit schematic, a resistor symbol is drawn with a diagonal arrow through it. What does the arrow indicate?
options: The conventional current in it flows along the arrow.
The resistance of the resistor can be adjusted.
The resistor is disconnected from the circuit.
The electrons move through it the way the arrow points.
optionWhy: A student who reads every arrow in a schematic as the direction of a current picks this. The diagonal arrow across a symbol marks a variable element; it says nothing about the direction of the current.
A diagonal arrow drawn through the standard symbol for an element marks it as a variable element; on a resistor symbol it shows a variable resistor, whose resistance can be adjusted.
A student who reads the diagonal line as crossing the element out picks this. The strikethrough arrow is the standard mark of a variable element, which is part of the circuit.

A student who reads arrows in a schematic as the direction of electron flow picks this. The diagonal arrow marks a variable element; and where a schematic does show a current, it is conventional current, not electron flow.
questions.explain: A diagonal arrow drawn through the standard symbol for an element marks it as a variable element; on a resistor symbol it shows a variable resistor, whose resistance can be adjusted.

questions.q: Resistor X has a greater resistance than resistor Y. Which statement about X and Y is correct?
options: With the same potential difference across each, X carries the smaller current.
Connected in turn across one ideal battery, X and Y carry equal currents.
X uses up more of the current entering it, so less current leaves X than leaves Y.
Whatever the potential differences across them, X has less current than Y.
optionWhy: Resistance measures how strongly an object opposes the movement of charge: R = ΔV/I is the potential difference needed per unit current. With the same ΔV across each, I = ΔV/R is smaller for the larger resistance, X.
A student who thinks a battery supplies a fixed current picks this. An ideal battery fixes the potential difference; with the same ΔV across each, the current I = ΔV/R is smaller in X.

A student who thinks a resistor uses up current picks this. Charge is conserved: the current leaving each resistor equals the current entering it. A larger resistance means a smaller current for a given ΔV, not a loss of current inside.
A student who thinks resistance alone fixes the current picks this. The current depends on ΔV as well: with a large enough potential difference across X, I = ΔV/R in X can exceed the current in Y.
questions.explain: Resistance measures how strongly an object opposes the movement of charge: R = ΔV/I is the potential difference needed per unit current. With the same ΔV across each, I = ΔV/R is smaller for the larger resistance, X.

questions.q: A copper wire is connected across an ideal battery. The wire is then cooled from 60 °C to 20 °C; its length and cross-sectional area change by negligible amounts. How do the wire's resistance and the current in it change as it cools?
options: The resistance increases, and the current decreases.
The resistance and the current both remain the same.
The resistance decreases; the current does not vary.
The resistance decreases, and the current increases.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a hot metal conducts better, so that cooling makes it conduct worse, picks this. For a metal the resistivity typically rises with temperature; cooling lowers it.
A student who thinks a wire's resistance is fixed by its length and area picks this. The resistivity itself depends on temperature, so the resistance changes even though the dimensions do not.
A student who thinks a battery supplies a fixed current picks this. The ideal battery fixes the potential difference; with a smaller resistance, I = ΔV/R is larger.

The resistivity of a conductor such as copper typically increases with temperature, so cooling the wire lowers its resistivity and, with ℓ and A unchanged, its resistance R = ρℓ/A. The battery keeps ΔV fixed, so I = ΔV/R increases.
questions.explain: The resistivity of a conductor such as copper typically increases with temperature, so cooling the wire lowers its resistivity and, with ℓ and A unchanged, its resistance R = ρℓ/A. The battery keeps ΔV fixed, so I = ΔV/R increases.

questions.q: The figure shows a hollow cylindrical resistor, in an end view and in a section along its axis, with its dimensions labeled. It is made of a material of uniform resistivity ρ. The current is along the length of the cylinder, spread uniformly over its wall. In terms of ρ, r and L, what is the resistance between the two ends?
options: ρL/(81πr²)
ρL/(16πr²)
ρL/(56πr²)
ρL/(72πr²)
optionWhy: A student who takes the cross-section of a hollow cylinder as a full circle of the outer radius, π(9r)² = 81πr², picks this. The core carries no current; the conducting area is the ring, 81πr² − 25πr² = 56πr².
A student who uses the wall thickness, 9r − 5r = 4r, as the radius in A = πr² picks this: π(4r)² = 16πr². That is the area of a circle of radius 4r, not the area of the ring.
The current passes along the length L through the wall only, so the cross-sectional area is that of the ring: A = π(9r)² − π(5r)² = 56πr². Then R = ρL/A = ρL/(56πr²).

A student who finds the ring's area as its outer circumference times its thickness, 2π(9r)(4r) = 72πr², picks this. That shortcut only approximates a thin ring; the exact area is 56πr², the thickness times the mean circumference 2π(7r).
questions.explain: The current passes along the length L through the wall only, so the cross-sectional area is that of the ring: A = π(9r)² − π(5r)² = 56πr². Then R = ρL/A = ρL/(56πr²).
questions.working: A = π(9r)² − π(5r)² = (81 − 25)πr² = 56πr²; R = ρL/A = ρL/(56πr²). All options have units Ω·m·m/m² = Ω. Distractors: full disk 81πr²; circle of radius 4r, 16πr²; outer circumference × thickness 2π(9r)(4r) = 72πr².

questions.q: Which condition must be met for two circuit elements to be connected in series with each other?
options: They are drawn one after the other along the same straight segment of wire in the circuit diagram.
They have equal potential differences across them whenever there is a current in the circuit.
Any charge passing through one of them must also pass through the other, having no other path.
They are joined to each other by a wire, even if other wires branch off between them.
optionWhy: A student who judges connections by the layout of the diagram picks this. Series and parallel are set by the paths available to charge: two elements drawn in a line can have a junction between them, and two elements on opposite sides of a diagram can be in series.

A student who thinks the battery's potential difference is shared equally picks this. Elements in series carry the same current, so their potential differences, ΔV = IR, are equal only if their resistances are equal.

This is what a series connection is: with no junction between the two elements, every charge that passes through one has no route except through the other. That is why elements in series always carry the same current.

A student who ignores junctions picks this. If a wire branches off between the two elements, charge passing through one can leave by the branch without passing through the other, so they are not in series.
questions.explain: This is what a series connection is: with no junction between the two elements, every charge that passes through one has no route except through the other. That is why elements in series always carry the same current.

questions.q: A group of resistors connected between two points has an equivalent resistance R_eq. Which statement describes what R_eq represents?
options: R_eq is the average of the resistances of all of the resistors in the group.
Every resistor in the group carries the current ΔV/R_eq, where ΔV is across the group.
R_eq is the sum of all the resistances in the group, however they are connected.
One resistor R_eq, across the same ΔV, would carry the same total current as the group.
optionWhy: A student who takes the equivalent resistance to be an average picks this. For resistors in series R_eq is the sum, larger than any of them; for resistors in parallel it is less than the smallest. Neither is an average.
A student who gives each resistor the equivalent resistor's current picks this. ΔV/R_eq is the TOTAL current into the group; in a parallel group it is shared among the paths.
A student who adds resistances whatever the connection picks this. Only resistances in series add; for resistors in parallel the reciprocals add, and R_eq is less than the smallest resistance.

The equivalent resistance is defined by replacement: a single resistor R_eq connected between the same two points, with the same potential difference ΔV, would carry the same total current, ΔV/R_eq, as the whole group.
questions.explain: The equivalent resistance is defined by replacement: a single resistor R_eq connected between the same two points, with the same potential difference ΔV, would carry the same total current, ΔV/R_eq, as the whole group.

questions.q: Which quantity is the emf ε of a nonideal battery?
options: The potential difference across its terminals while it supplies its largest current
The potential difference across its terminals when there is no current in it
The force that the battery exerts on each of the charges that pass through it
The total amount of charge that the battery is able to deliver before running down
optionWhy: A student who takes the emf to be the terminal potential difference while the battery is working picks this. With current I, the terminal potential difference is ε − Ir, which is at its smallest, not equal to ε, when the current is largest.

The emf is the potential difference the battery would supply if it were ideal. With no current in the battery there is no potential difference across its internal resistance (Ir = 0), so the terminal potential difference then equals ε.
A student misled by the name 'electromotive force' picks this. Emf is measured in volts: it is a potential difference, energy per unit charge, not a force.

A student who pictures a battery as a store of charge picks this. A battery separates charge already present in the circuit; its emf, in volts, is the potential difference it would maintain with no current, not a quantity of charge.
questions.explain: The emf is the potential difference the battery would supply if it were ideal. With no current in the battery there is no potential difference across its internal resistance (Ir = 0), so the terminal potential difference then equals ε.

questions.q: A small positive test charge is carried once around a circuit consisting of an ideal battery, ideal wires and one resistor, in the direction of the conventional current. Which statement correctly describes the electric potential energy of the test charge?
options: It increases in the battery and decreases steadily along both the wires and the resistor.
It decreases in the resistor, where part of the test charge itself is used up.
It stays the same all the way around, because the current is the same everywhere.
It increases in the battery and decreases by the same amount in the resistor.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the potential falls along every part of the circuit picks this. Ideal wires have negligible resistance, so the potential is the same all along each wire; the whole decrease is in the resistor.
A student who thinks charge is used up in a resistor picks this. The charge passes through the resistor unchanged; what it gives up is electric potential energy.

A student who thinks a constant current means constant energy picks this. The current is the same in every part of a single loop, but the potential, and with it the charge's potential energy, rises in the battery and falls in the resistor.

In the battery the charge moves from the − to the + terminal, to a higher potential, so its electric potential energy increases by qε. Along ideal wires the potential does not change. In the resistor it moves to a lower potential and loses qε, the same amount, so it returns with its starting energy.
questions.explain: In the battery the charge moves from the − to the + terminal, to a higher potential, so its electric potential energy increases by qε. Along ideal wires the potential does not change. In the resistor it moves to a lower potential and loses qε, the same amount, so it returns with its starting energy.

questions.q: A battery with an emf of 12.0 V and an internal resistance of 1.0 Ω drives a current of 2.0 A through an external resistor. How much electric energy is transferred to the external resistor as 5.0 C of charge passes through it?
optionWhy: The potential difference across the external resistor equals the terminal potential difference: ε − Ir = 12.0 V − (2.0 A)(1.0 Ω) = 10.0 V. Each coulomb passing through the resistor loses 10.0 J of electric potential energy, so ΔU_E = qΔV = (5.0 C)(10.0 V) = 50 J.

A student who takes the full emf, 12.0 V, to be across the external resistor gets (5.0 C)(12.0 V) = 60 J. The battery's internal resistance takes Ir = 2.0 V of the emf, leaving 10.0 V for the external resistor.

A student who shares the emf equally between the internal and external resistances gives each 6.0 V and gets (5.0 C)(6.0 V) = 30 J. The shares are in proportion to the resistances: Ir = 2.0 V across the internal resistance, 10.0 V across the external resistor.
A student who takes the potential difference across the resistor, 10.0 V, as the energy transferred picks this. A volt is a joule per coulomb, so 5.0 C passing through 10.0 V transfers 50 J.
questions.explain: The potential difference across the external resistor equals the terminal potential difference: ε − Ir = 12.0 V − (2.0 A)(1.0 Ω) = 10.0 V. Each coulomb passing through the resistor loses 10.0 J of electric potential energy, so ΔU_E = qΔV = (5.0 C)(10.0 V) = 50 J.
questions.working: ΔV_ext = ε − Ir = 12.0 − 2.0 × 1.0 = 10.0 V. ΔU_E = qΔV = 5.0 × 10.0 = 50 J. (Full emf: 60 J; equal split: 30 J; ΔV as energy: 10 J.)

questions.q: The circuit shown contains two ideal batteries and two resistors in a single loop. In terms of ε and R, what is the magnitude of the current in the loop?
optionWhy: A student who adds the two emfs whatever their orientation gets (3ε + ε)/(5R). The + terminals of the two batteries face the same way on the page, so around the loop they oppose each other: the net emf is 3ε − ε.

Going clockwise around the loop, up through the 3ε battery (− to +): +3ε; down through the ε battery (+ to −): −ε; and −I(2R) − I(3R) across the resistors. Loop rule: 3ε − ε − 5IR = 0, so I = 2ε/(5R) = (2/5)ε/R, clockwise.

A student who treats 2R and 3R as parallel, because they are drawn in separate vertical branches, uses R_eq = 6R/5 and gets 2ε/(6R/5). Each resistor is in series with a battery in its branch, and the loop is a single path, so the resistors are in series: R_eq = 5R.

A student who takes the current to be set by the 3ε battery and the resistor in its own branch alone gets 3ε/(2R). The current is the same all around the single loop and is set by the net emf and the total resistance.
questions.explain: Going clockwise around the loop, up through the 3ε battery (− to +): +3ε; down through the ε battery (+ to −): −ε; and −I(2R) − I(3R) across the resistors. Loop rule: 3ε − ε − 5IR = 0, so I = 2ε/(5R) = (2/5)ε/R, clockwise.
questions.working: Clockwise: +3ε − I(3R) − ε − I(2R) = 0 → I = 2ε/(5R). (Emfs added: 4ε/(5R); resistors treated as parallel: 2ε/(6R/5) = 5ε/(3R); local: 3ε/(2R).)

questions.q: Which statement correctly explains why Kirchhoff’s junction rule holds?
options: Energy is conserved, so the energy carried into a junction each second equals that carried out.
Charge is conserved and does not build up at a junction, so it leaves as fast as it arrives.
Currents are vectors, so the currents in the wires that meet at a junction add as arrows to zero.
A battery drives the same current through every wire, so all the currents at a junction match.
optionWhy: A student who links the junction rule to the conservation of energy picks this. Energy conservation underlies the loop rule; the junction rule follows from the conservation of charge.

The junction rule is a consequence of the conservation of charge. Charge is neither created nor destroyed at a junction and, in a steady state, does not accumulate there, so the charge entering per unit time equals the charge leaving per unit time.
A student who treats current as a vector picks this. Current is a scalar with a direction along each wire; the angles between the wires play no part, only whether each current is in or out.
A student who thinks the current is the same in every wire of a circuit picks this. At a junction the current divides, and the branch currents add up to the incoming current; they are not all equal.
questions.explain: The junction rule is a consequence of the conservation of charge. Charge is neither created nor destroyed at a junction and, in a steady state, does not accumulate there, so the charge entering per unit time equals the charge leaving per unit time.

questions.q: The diagram shows three wires meeting at junction P. The currents in two of the wires and their directions are shown. What are the magnitude and direction of the current I₃ in the third wire?
options: 1.8 A out of P
4.2 A out of P
1.2 A out of P
3.0 A out of P
optionWhy: Into P: 3.0 A. Out of P: 1.2 A plus I₃. The junction rule, ΣI_in = ΣI_out, gives 3.0 A = 1.2 A + I₃, so I₃ = 1.8 A, directed out of P.
A student who adds the magnitudes of the other two currents without regard to their directions picks this: 3.0 A + 1.2 A. The 1.2 A current already leaves P, so it belongs on the 'out' side with I₃.

A student who thinks the current divides equally among the wires leaving a junction picks this, giving I₃ the same value as the other outgoing current. The currents out must add up to the 3.0 A coming in: 1.2 A + 1.8 A.

A student who thinks the incoming current carries straight on along the continuing wire picks this. The layout does not matter: 1.2 A of the 3.0 A leaves by the side wire, so 1.8 A remains for the third wire.
questions.explain: Into P: 3.0 A. Out of P: 1.2 A plus I₃. The junction rule, ΣI_in = ΣI_out, gives 3.0 A = 1.2 A + I₃, so I₃ = 1.8 A, directed out of P.
questions.working: ΣI_in = ΣI_out: 3.0 A = 1.2 A + I₃ → I₃ = 1.8 A out of P.
